title: Democracy and Empire
abstract: Democracy and Empire theorizes the material basis of popular sovereignty via the Black radical tradition. Popular sovereignty contains an affective attachment to wealth, secured through collective agreements to dominate others, i.e., self-and-other-determination. Inés Valdez expands on racial capitalism by theorizing its Anglo-European-based popular politics, which authorize capital accumulation enabled by empire and legitimated by racial ideologies. This stunts political projects in the Global South. Valdez masterfully outlines how social reproduction is provided by racialized others who sacrifice families and communities, and how the political alienation from nature in wealthy polities is mediated by technology and enabled by a joint devaluation of nature and manual labor performed by racialized others. The book concludes with a theorization of anti-imperial popular sovereignty based on political relations that encompass nature. This title is part of the Flip it Open Programme and may also be available Open Access. Check our website Cambridge Core for details.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Democracy and Empire shows strong scholarly uptake, with 51 citations and standing in the top 1% of works in its field and publication year. Its influence is concentrated in political theory, political philosophy, sociology, and adjacent debates on race, capitalism, sovereignty, and empire, with additional alignment to the Sustainable Development Goal on decent work and economic growth.

Full narrative

Inés Valdez’s Democracy and Empire has already attracted measurable academic attention, registering 51 citations in OpenAlex and ranking in the top 1% of cited works for its field and year. The citing record suggests that the book is being taken up where questions of popular sovereignty, racial capitalism, political economy, and empire are actively debated, especially in political theory and related humanities and social science fields.

The citation landscape is broad but intellectually focused. The largest share of citing work appears in journals and books across political theory, political philosophy, sociology, migration studies, race and history, and political economy. This pattern fits the book’s argument that democracy and empire are not separable domains but mutually constitutive, and it indicates that the book is informing discussion well beyond a single niche.

The work’s reach is strongest in education-based institutions, with citing authors and institutions concentrated in universities in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, alongside additional references from other countries. The most visible venues include Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy, Contemporary Political Theory, European Journal of Political Theory, American Political Science Review, and American Journal of Political Science, pointing to sustained engagement in high-level scholarly conversation.

There are also signs of practical and public-facing relevance, though the record is more limited there than for citations. The book is available openly through an OpenAIRE-listed open instance, and its subject profile connects it to political science and history in library holdings. It is also associated with an SDG link to decent work and economic growth, which suggests relevance to broader questions of economic order and power, even if the strongest evidence in the record remains scholarly uptake.

Overall, the available evidence portrays Democracy and Empire as an influential intervention in contemporary debates on sovereignty, empire, democracy, and racial capitalism. The citation pattern is still developing, but the current record already shows clear academic traction, especially among scholars working at the intersection of political theory, critical social theory, and histories of capitalism and race.
